client: I've been dreading this family reunion coming up next month. Ever since that huge fight with my cousin last year, just thinking about seeing them again makes my chest feel tight and my hands start shaking. I keep playing that awful argument over in my head, wondering if everyone's still mad at me.
therapist: It sounds like this upcoming reunion is bringing up a lot of anxiety for you, especially with the painful memories of last year's argument still feeling so fresh. When you notice your body reacting with tightness and shaking, what thoughts tend to go through your mind in those moments?

client: I keep thinking everyone will judge me and take my cousin's side. I worry that I'll say something wrong again and make things worse. It feels like no matter what I do, I can't fix this mess.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of worry about how others might perceive you, and that fear of making things worse feels paralyzing. Have you noticed any times when you've successfully navigated a tense situation, or when your fears about judgment didn't come true?

client: Actually, now that you mention it... I did have coffee with an old friend who I thought was still mad at me from a misunderstanding. It went okay - she wasn't angry at all. But this feels different because it's the whole family, not just one person. What if I'm the only one who still feels awkward about it?
therapist: It's interesting that you noticed things went better than expected with your friend, even though this family situation feels heavier because there are more people involved. That moment with your friend shows our predictions aren't always accurate—what makes you think this family situation might follow a completely different pattern?

client: I guess I'm assuming the family situation is different because it felt so public when we argued, with everyone watching. At least with my friend it was just between us two. But you're right, maybe I'm jumping to worst-case scenarios again. It's just hard to imagine them not still being upset.
therapist: It makes sense that the public nature of the family argument makes it feel harder to move past—those visible moments can leave deeper marks. I notice your tone has shifted slightly from panic to more thoughtful concern, which is a great space for us to work in. What would it look like to test whether your family members are actually still upset, rather than assuming they are?

client: I could maybe text my sister first—she wasn't directly involved but knows everyone. But I'm scared she'll tell me they are still mad, and then I'll have to dread it even more. Part of me thinks ignorance might be better than knowing for sure.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting information and fearing what you might learn—that's such an understandable dilemma when we're facing uncertainty. What do you imagine would be the most helpful way your sister could respond, if you did decide to reach out to her?

client: I guess the best response would be if she said everyone's moved on and it's not a big deal anymore. But that feels too good to be true. Honestly, I'm not sure if I even trust her to tell me the truth—what if she's just saying that to make me feel better?
therapist: I hear that hopeful but cautious part of you that wants this tension to be resolved, and also that distrustful part that worries about being given false reassurance—that's a difficult space to be in. When you think about your sister's past behavior, has she typically avoided difficult truths to protect your feelings?

client: Actually, my sister has always been pretty blunt—sometimes too honest if anything. I remember last Christmas she told me straight up when my outfit wasn't flattering. Maybe I'm projecting my own discomfort onto her. But even if she's honest, hearing the truth might still hurt.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing that your sister has a history of being direct—even when it's uncomfortable—which actually might make her a reliable source in this situation. That awareness about possibly projecting your discomfort shows real self-reflection. How might you prepare yourself emotionally if you decide to reach out to her, knowing the answer might be difficult but honest?

client: I guess I could remind myself that whatever she says, I've handled tough situations before and I'll get through this too. But it's still scary—what if she confirms my worst fears and says the family is still upset? I'm not sure I'm ready to face that yet.
therapist: That mix of courage and fear you're describing—knowing you could handle it but not being sure you're ready—shows how deeply you're thinking this through. What would it look like to approach this gradually, maybe starting with a less direct question to your sister to test the waters first?

client: I could ask something casual like "Are people still talking about last year's drama?" But even typing that out makes my hands sweat. What if she says yes and then I have to deal with that knowledge for weeks before the reunion? Maybe I should just wait and see how things are when I get there.
therapist: I hear how even considering this conversation is creating physical anxiety for you—that shows how important this family dynamic is to you. It might help to notice that your suggestion of a casual question shows you're finding a middle ground between avoidance and diving straight into difficult topics. What small step could you take today to build your confidence, even if you decide not to reach out right away?

client: Maybe I could practice deep breathing first—I know that helps sometimes when I get anxious. But I'm not sure it'll make a difference with something this big. It feels like the anxiety is too deep for simple breathing tricks to touch it.
therapist: It's great that you're recognizing breathing could help, while also acknowledging this feels bigger than quick fixes—that balance shows real self-awareness. When you notice those moments of deep anxiety, what other grounding techniques have helped you in the past, even if just a little?
